learningObjective: Identify the impact of a large stride on effective global-memory bandwidth utilization in a warp-wide load.

canonicalClaims.claim: When lanes of a warp access global memory with stride S in the element index, each L1/L2 sector transaction delivers roughly one useful element per S; effective bandwidth utilization is approximately 1/S of peak until reads spread over multiple sectors.
conditions: L1/L2 sector granularity ≥ warp's per-lane load size × warp size (32 threads on NVIDIA).
No SW-level reordering (e.g., swizzling) has been introduced to re-coalesce.
nonImplications: Does not imply that stride > 1 always kills bandwidth to 0; if the stride keeps requests within a small number of sectors, some bandwidth is still delivered.
Does not imply that stride is intrinsic to the algorithm; often a layout change (transpose, permute) can restore coalescing.

misconceptions.claim: Strided global-memory access causes bank conflicts.
misconceptions.whyWrong: Bank conflicts are a shared-memory concept; global memory has coalescing/sectoring instead.

misconceptions.claim: Applying a mask to `tl.load` eliminates the bandwidth penalty of strided access.
misconceptions.whyWrong: Masking removes OOB traffic; among valid lanes, the sectoring loss is unchanged.
`cp.async` hides latency by overlapping compute and copy; it does not increase the number of useful bytes per sector transaction.
misconceptions.sourceOrEvidence: CUDA C++ Programming Guide, cp.async section

misconceptions.claim: For FP32 with warp size 32, any stride < 32 has no measurable impact on bandwidth utilization.
misconceptions.whyWrong: Even stride 2 doubles the number of sectors touched and typically halves effective bandwidth for streaming reads.

implementationFacts: sm_80 typical L2/L1 sector: 32 B, transactions grouped to 128 B
Warp of 32 threads accessing FP32 with stride 1 fits into 128 B (fully coalesced)
Warp accessing FP32 with stride S spans up to 32*S bytes
performanceScenarios: Strided reads are common in gather/scatter patterns; refactoring the layout (or performing a coalesced load into SMEM followed by transpose) restores coalescing.
Naive matrix transposes suffer from strided writes; the standard SMEM-tile pattern (with padding to avoid bank conflicts) converts stride into contiguity at the SMEM level.
